title: From woman we are born
hookLine: Guru Nanak asks why she should be called lesser, from whom kings are born (Asa di Var, ang 473)
tomorrow: Ask about the light, not the caste

cards: A baby is born, and in Guru Nanak's world, some said the birth had made the whole house unclean, the mother most of all. It was simply how things were said.
Then a traveling teacher with a musician at his side sings a verse that asks one question, so plainly it's hard to argue with. It's in the Asa di Var, the morning ballad: from woman we are born.

teach.h: ASA DI VAR — THE MORNING BALLAD.
teach.b: The Asa di Var is a long hymn sung in many gurdwaras in the early morning. On Ang 473 comes a salok by Guru Nanak. It begins with a drumbeat of one word, bhand, woman.
In paraphrase: from woman we are born; in woman we are conceived; to woman we are engaged and married. Through woman comes friendship; through woman the way of the world goes on.
When one woman dies, a man seeks another; through woman come our bonds with the world. Then the question, in the original: so kio mandaa aakheeai jit jameh raajaan.
Why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? The salok goes on: from woman, woman is born; without woman there is no one at all. Only the One, the True Lord, Nanak says, is beyond woman.
Notice where this sits. The verses just before it are about ritual impurity, sutak, the belief that birth made a house unclean.
Guru Nanak answers that impurity lives in greed, lies and gossip, not in a newborn or a mother. So this isn't a greeting-card compliment.

teach.h: AN ARGUMENT ABOUT WHO IS CLEAN.
teach.b: It's an argument, set in the middle of a debate about who is clean.
Sikh practice reads the verse that way: in the sangat, women and men sit together and eat together in the langar, and women may read from the Guru Granth Sahib and lead prayers.
Honesty belongs here too: life hasn't always matched the verse. But the verse is there, sung in the morning, still asking.

how: The Asa di Var is sung in many gurdwaras as part of the early-morning program; in Sikh congregations women and men sit together, eat together in the langar, and women may read from the Guru Granth Sahib and lead prayers.

games.q: people around Guru Nanak say a house is made unclean by a birth. what does the Asa di Var answer?
o: that they're right, and women should keep apart.
that impurity lives in greed, lies and gossip, and asks why she should be called lesser, from whom kings are born.
games.why: Guru Nanak moves impurity from the body to behavior, then asks: so kio mandaa aakheeai jit jameh raajaan.

practice: Bring to mind a woman in your life, a mother, a grandmother, a sister, a friend, a teacher, a colleague, and picture her face. Think of one thing she carried that nobody thanked her for, and hold that for a moment.
Rest with the breath, and keep her in mind.

wordCard.voice: Bhand, woman. Guru Nanak's salok in the Asa di Var: everyone comes through woman, so why call her lesser, from whom kings are born?

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhand, an old Punjabi word for woman; the salok repeats it like a drumbeat.

carryVoice: Your line: why call her lesser. One plain question, hard to argue with. Day two hundred forty-seven, in the books.
